newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus deal collapses, Lukashenko defiant.
newsitem.headline: Belarus deal collapses, Lukashenko defiant.

text.p: Hardline President Alexander Lukashenko and parliament in Belarus turned their backs on a day-old political deal on Saturday, throwing the former Soviet republic into fresh political crisis.
Lukashenko, comparing deputies to animals in a zoo, said in a television interview that he had cancelled his half of the deal, brokered by neighbouring Russia.
He announced that a controversial referendum on Sunday on increasing his powers would be mandatory, and scheduled a television address to the nation at nine p.m. (1900 GMT).

Meanwhile deputies went to the constitutional court to recommence impeachment proceedings against him and parliamentary speaker Semyon Sharetsky, who signed the agreement, accused the president of lying.

"The situation in Belarus is getting worse and tensions are growing. We thought we would be able to calm the storm. But the president wanted and still wants to grab more power by anti- constitutional means," he told a news conference.
Each side blamed the other for the collapse of the agreement, which deputies failed to pass at a late-night session on Friday despite two addresses from Lukashenko.

The development was a serious loss of face for Russian President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from a heart operation, who sent Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to broker the accord in all-night talks between Thursday and Friday.

"The referendum will have a mandatory character. I declare this directly since neither the parliament nor the constitutional court has fulfilled the obligations which they took on," Lukashenko said, ruling out any further attempts at compromise.

He said parliament's failure to pass the deal showed disrespect to everyone involved, including Russia, which hailed the accord as a great success for its diplomacy and for the "community" it formed with Belarus last April.
But Sharetsky dismissed this. "As before, he is using lies to seize power. He had no sympathy with anyone, not even sick Yeltsin and leading Russian politicians," he said.
Lukashenko recalled his visit to parliament, where debates raged all day on Friday and one of his supporters tried to grab the microphone after another deputy called Lukashenko a tyrant.

"Excuse me, but it was like a menagerie," he whispered, leaning closer to the interviewer. "Three at the back shouting, another one shouting on the left, another one jumping, someone hollering, someone whistling," he said.
The Russians had been kind enough to come to Minsk and mediate in the signing of the agreement, he said, "and then they (the parliament) just threw it in the bin."

It was not clear if Lukashenko had consulted Russia, his closest ally and guarantor of the agreement, before deciding to cancel the deal but Moscow's ambassador in an interview with Reuters described the situation as "very bad".

"Lukashenko is a wise enough politician to solve his domestic problems by himself but I do not exclude the possibility that Russia will try again to solve this crisis," the ambassador, Igor Saprykin, said.
Yeltsin's spokesman said on Saturday the president considered Friday's compromise as the first key step in ending the conflict, despite its apparent failure.
"Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) considers there is no need to jump to conclusions. He very much counts on the process of fulfilling the agreement being continued and brought to a conclusion."
Meanwhile the constitutional court, which has repeatedly ruled that Lukashensko has exceeded his powers, was meeting deputies who brought a new request to impeach Lukashenko.

Amid uncertainty over how many deputies still supported impeachment, the court decided to adjourn until Tuesday, when parliament is next due to meet. A deputy who attended the session said one judge was absent and the court was split 5-5.
"The president has scared the judges. Now the court will bear moral responsibility for whatever happens to parliament," the deputy, Alexander Dobrovolsky said.
Lukashenko wants to use the referendum to tighten his grip on rival institutions and extend his term by more than two years -- an idea fiercely opposed by parliament.
Parliament, due to meet again on Tuesday, now faces the risk that Lukashenko will either ignore it or order it dissolved if voters, as expected, approve his constitutional draft.
Western officials and his opponents have observed serious flaws in early voting which began almost two weeks ago on November 9. The situation in Minsk on Saturday remained calm.
